value_chain_position: Prime shipbuilder/integrator for naval nuclear-propulsion vessels -- occupies the chain's 'reactor components & naval/defense nuclear' layer at the platform-EPC level, not as a fuel or component sub-supplier.
cost_curve_verified: Disagree, materially. Our deterministic screener proxy reports trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of $376 million on capital spending of $29 million; the company's own filings show capital spending of $119 million in the second quarter of 2026 alone (3.5% of revenue, against a roughly 4% full-year guide) and first-half 2026 free cash flow of about negative $614 million, leaving trailing free cash flow close to zero. Use the company figures: 2026 free-cash-flow guidance of $500-600 million, reiterated on 30 July 2026, with about $100 million guided for the third quarter -- which loads roughly $1.0-1.1 billion onto the fourth quarter.
gm_trajectory: Modestly expanding on strongly growing revenue. Trailing-twelve-month gross margin is 12.56% versus 12.38% a year earlier while revenue grew about 14% to $13.19 billion; in the second quarter of 2026 alone gross margin was 13.2% against 12.8% a year earlier, and segment operating margin rose to 6.6% from 5.6%. That is pricing power improving, but from a very low base and driven by contract mix and incentive fees rather than price -- shipbuilding return on sales has marched 5.2% (2024) to 5.9% (2025) to 6.0-6.5% guided (2026), still far from management's 9-10% long-term goal.
bull_thesis:
Huntington Ingalls builds the ships nobody else in America can build, and after two painful years the arithmetic has finally turned in its favour. It is the sole builder of nuclear-powered aircraft carriers in the United States and one of only two builders of nuclear submarines. The barriers -- licensing, security clearances, dry docks, and a 44,000-person skilled workforce -- cannot be replicated by anyone at any price on a relevant timescale.

The core of the bull case is a mechanical margin recovery that is already visible in the numbers. For four years HII has been building ships priced before the pandemic, at pre-pandemic assumptions about labour and material cost, and losing money against those assumptions. Management set out the crossover date -- 2027, when post-pandemic contracts exceed pre-pandemic work -- in the third quarter of 2025, and when Goldman Sachs asked in the first quarter of 2026 whether that schedule had drifted, the chief financial officer answered that the current and year-ago plans 'look on top of each other right now.' The recovery is showing up on schedule: shipbuilding return on sales went 5.2% in 2024, 5.9% in 2025, and is now guided to 6.0-6.5% for 2026, with the quarterly sequence marching 5.8%, 6.0%, 6.3%. On the 30 July 2026 call management raised both shipbuilding revenue guidance (to $10.2-10.4 billion from $9.7-9.9 billion) and the margin floor (to 6.0% from 5.5%) in the same release -- the fourth consecutive quarter of double-digit shipbuilding growth.

The single largest overhang closed on 29 July 2026. After roughly eighteen months of slippage, the US Navy awarded $76.6 billion across nine Block VI Virginia-class attack submarines (with material bought for a tenth) and five Columbia-class Build II ballistic-missile submarines, running to July 2038. About $25 billion of that flows to Newport News, about $5.5 billion sits on the Columbia programme, and roughly $5 billion is earmarked across both builders for shipyard productivity, workforce and industrial-base investment. That last item matters more than it looks: it means the customer is funding a large share of HII's growth capital spending, which is why capital expenditure can run at 3.5-4% of sales instead of the 2.5% long-run norm without wrecking free cash flow. The chief executive's characterisation of the terms -- 'I do obviously expect it to perform better than those contracts... very consistent with the long term margin profile that we expect' -- is the whole thesis in one sentence.

Demand is about as certain as anything in equities. Backlog was $57.3 billion at 30 June 2026, roughly 4.3 times trailing revenue, with second-quarter book-to-bill (orders divided by revenue) of 1.96 times -- and that is before the July submarine modifications book in the third quarter, which should take backlog toward $80 billion, or about six years of revenue. Named, dated milestones sit in front of the stock: CVN 79 Kennedy preliminary acceptance later in 2026 with delivery in 2027, SSN 800 Arkansas delivery late 2026, LPD 30 Harrisburg delivery in 2026, the CVN 81 keel laying in the back half of 2026, and five ships delivered over the next twelve months. Funding is bipartisan and appropriated: the fiscal-2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act funds CVN 80 and 81 with advance procurement for CVN 82, and the fiscal-2027 request adds two amphibious ships, two Block VI submarines, one Columbia, the first FFX frigate and initial money for a new battleship class.

Two option values are explicitly excluded from guidance. Ingalls won the frigate lead-yard-support contract in April 2026 (long-lead material, design work, pre-construction), and the announced battleship programme has advance procurement in the fiscal-2027 request. Management refused to include either: 'we will need additional details before we can include those in our guidance outlook.' Separately, Mission Technologies has crossed from pilot to production in unmanned systems -- the 750th REMUS undersea vehicle delivered, the next Lionfish production option secured, and the ROMULUS unmanned surface vessel advanced to Navy medium-unmanned-surface-vessel at-sea testing scheduled for September 2026.

The labour problem, which was the real constraint, is being fixed with dated actions rather than promises: a Newport News wage adjustment in mid-2025, an Ingalls collective bargaining agreement signed in March 2026 with 'immediate benefit from a retention standpoint,' 6,600 shipbuilders hired in 2025 and over 3,500 in the first half of 2026, apprentice schools at full enrolment, and distributed shipbuilding across 23-plus partner yards growing 30% in 2026.

Finally, valuation. At $324.21 the shares trade on about 10.2 times consensus 2028 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation and 13.5 times 2028 consensus earnings per share of $23.94. General Dynamics -- whose Electric Boat unit is the direct submarine peer -- trades at about 17 times trailing enterprise value to that same measure, and BWX Technologies, the naval reactor-components supplier, at about 33 times. Simply delivering the plan without any multiple change gets the shares to the high $300s.

Conditions that must hold: shipbuilding margin keeps grinding toward 7.5-8% by 2028; the fourth-quarter 2026 cash-flow catch-up arrives; no large adverse contract re-estimate on a carrier or a Block V boat; and defence appropriations continue through the fiscal-2027 and 2028 cycles without a prolonged funding lapse.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not need demand to fail. It needs only two things that have both already happened to this company inside the last two years.

First, reported profit here is a management estimate, not a measured result. Under percentage-of-completion accounting, margin depends on judgements about costs still four to six years out. When those judgements reset, the reset is violent and instant. On 31 October 2024 the shares fell 26% in a single session, from $250.49 to $184.96. On 6 February 2025 they fell another 18%, from $195.58 to $159.75, bottoming near $160 in mid-February -- a 36% decline in roughly three months, driven entirely by adverse contract re-estimates. Newport News still carried a negative 13% net estimate adjustment as recently as the third quarter of 2025. Nothing structural has retired that mechanism; it has merely been quiet for four quarters. Management themselves conceded on the 30 July 2026 call that 'a piece of Q2 has incentives in there' and then twice declined to size the submarine-contract adjustment -- 'we normally do not provide that type of visibility.' Investors therefore cannot separate how much of the 6.6% segment margin was operational improvement and how much was a one-time credit.

Second, the 2026 cash-flow guide is now an extraordinary ask. First-half 2026 free cash flow was roughly negative $614 million (operating cash flow of negative $390 million in the first quarter and negative $31 million in the second, against net capital spending of $74 million and $119 million). The third quarter is guided to only about $100 million. To reach the reiterated $500-600 million full-year range, the fourth quarter must produce roughly $1.0-1.1 billion in a single quarter -- about double the $516 million achieved in the fourth quarter of 2025. Management's support for that is 'contract advances and incentives' from a contract signed on 29 July and 'favorable cash tax impacts' from a research-and-development credit. If the advances slip one quarter, the guide breaks publicly in February 2027, and this is a company that ended the second quarter with a $12 million cash balance against $2.92 billion of net debt including capitalised leases ($2.69 billion excluding them). Its $1.7 billion of liquidity is almost entirely undrawn revolving credit, not cash.

Third -- and this is the input-cost channel that matters for an equipment maker, because it is labour rather than copper -- HII has just reset wages twice: at Newport News in mid-2025 and at Ingalls under a new collective bargaining agreement in March 2026. Every dollar of wage inflation above the assumption embedded in an existing estimate-at-completion is a direct, immediate margin charge on the pre-pandemic book that still represents the majority of work in progress. The chief executive was explicit in May 2025 that broad wage moves were constrained by labour arrangements; those constraints have now been renegotiated upward. Steel, copper and specialty-alloy inflation runs through the same channel on a book that has no escalation protection on its older contracts.

Fourth, the political ground under the largest asset is genuinely moving. Within these six quarters we have a presidential review of aircraft-carrier design, a proposal to revert catapults from electromagnetic to steam, the Shipbuilder Accountability and Workforce Support provision cut from the final maritime executive order, and a wholly new battleship class appearing in the fiscal-2027 request. Kastner's answer to the carrier-design question -- 'we're going to build whatever the Navy asks us to build' -- is honest and also exactly the problem: HII is a price-taker to a single customer whose preferences are now volatile. The fiscal-2027 budget is a request, not law. A prolonged continuing resolution, or a rotation of the shipbuilding account toward distributed and unmanned platforms, flattens the revenue ramp that the entire re-rating depends on. Note also that the September-October 2025 funding lapse already halted much of the government; HII escaped because shipbuilding was one of six protected priorities, which is a policy choice, not a guarantee.

Fifth, the returns simply do not justify a premium multiple, and never have. Return on invested capital is 5.3% and return on equity 12.9%, against General Dynamics at 10.9% and 17.4%. A monopoly that earns 5% on capital is a monopoly whose surplus is being captured by its single buyer. Even if management reaches its 9-10% shipbuilding margin ambition -- four or more years away and entirely unproven -- return on invested capital gets to perhaps 9-10%, which is respectable, not exceptional. The 'discount' to General Dynamics is a quality discount and is largely deserved.

Sixth, the price has already moved. The shares jumped about 12% on the second-quarter print and sit roughly 11% above their 50-day average of $292 and about 25% above the 52-week low of $259. The two most recent published price targets -- Bernstein at $337 on 17 July and Wells Fargo at $325 on 8 July -- were both set before the result and are already at or below the current price. Coverage is thin: only two targets printed last quarter against nine over the past year. Meanwhile insiders have made zero open-market purchases against four sales of 14,100 shares, and the company bought back no stock at all in the second quarter.

What would confirm the bear: a negative net estimate-at-completion adjustment of more than $50 million at Newport News in the third or fourth quarter of 2026; fourth-quarter free cash flow below about $800 million; a fiscal-2027 continuing resolution running past January 2027; or any slippage in the CVN 79 preliminary-acceptance or SSN 800 delivery dates.
sop_bull:
$497 per share (favourable case, valuing the parts on 2028 earnings power). Assumes shipbuilding margin reaches about 8.5% by 2028 -- ahead of the current 6.0-6.5% but still below management's 9-10% goal -- and that the unmanned franchise inside Mission Technologies earns a defence-technology multiple.

- Newport News Shipbuilding: about $8.1 billion of revenue at an 10.6% margin on earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, roughly $860 million, at 14 times = $12.0 billion. The 14 times reflects a sole-source nuclear franchise with contracted work to 2038, still a discount to General Dynamics at about 17 times trailing.
- Ingalls Shipbuilding: about $3.8 billion of revenue (destroyers, amphibious ships, plus the FFX frigate and battleship ramping) at a 10.5% margin, roughly $400 million, at 12 times = $4.8 billion.
- Mission Technologies: about $3.45 billion of revenue at a 10% margin, roughly $345 million, at 15 times = $5.2 billion -- a re-rating on the unmanned and autonomy portfolio (REMUS, Lionfish, ROMULUS, the Odyssey software stack) toward defence-technology peers.
- Overlays: overfunded pension surplus roughly +$0.6 billion, net corporate cost capitalised at roughly -$0.5 billion, net +$0.1 billion.

Enterprise value $22.1 billion, less net debt of about $2.6 billion (declining as free cash flow recovers), gives equity of about $19.5 billion on roughly 39.2 million shares = $497 per share. Sanity check: that is about 20.7 times 2028 consensus earnings per share of $23.94, against General Dynamics on roughly 23 times trailing, and it is 8% above the 52-week high of $460 the shares reached earlier this cycle.
sop_bear:
$180 per share (adverse case, assuming the naval-nuclear build cycle turns against it). Assumes a prolonged federal funding lapse or continuing resolution flattens the revenue ramp, wage and material inflation from the 2025 Newport News adjustment and the March 2026 Ingalls agreement runs through the pre-pandemic contract book as negative estimate-at-completion charges, and the multiple reverts toward where HII actually traded in early 2025.

- Newport News Shipbuilding: revenue stalls near $7.3 billion, margin on earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation falls back to 7.5%, roughly $548 million, at 10.0 times = $5.48 billion.
- Ingalls Shipbuilding: revenue about $3.4 billion (frigate and battleship deferred), 8.0% margin, roughly $272 million, at 9.0 times = $2.45 billion.
- Mission Technologies: revenue about $3.05 billion under services-budget pressure (the segment already shrank 3.9% year over year in the second quarter of 2026), 8.0% margin, roughly $244 million, at 10.5 times = $2.56 billion.
- Overlays: pension credit shrinks on a rate or asset shock and net corporate cost is unchanged, roughly -$0.2 billion.

Enterprise value $10.29 billion, less net debt rising to about $3.2 billion as the revolving credit facility is drawn after a fourth-quarter cash miss, gives equity of about $7.09 billion on roughly 39.5 million shares = $180 per share.

Calibration: this is a 44% decline, which is precisely the drawdown the shares suffered over the last twelve months (from a high of $460 to a low of $259) and close to the 36% three-month decline of October 2024 to February 2025. It is an adverse case, not a tail. The genuine tail -- a single-session estimate-at-completion blow-up of the kind seen on 31 October 2024, layered on top of the above -- reaches roughly $145.
sop_breakdown:
Base case values each business on its own 2028-2029 earnings power and its own peer multiple, then nets the balance sheet.

- Newport News Shipbuilding (about 52% of revenue): roughly $8.2 billion of revenue at an 8.0% margin on earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, about $656 million, at 13.0 times = $8.53 billion. Thirteen times sits between General Dynamics (about 17 times, richer mix and double the returns) and a plain conventional shipbuilder (about 9-10 times). It is justified by the sole-source nuclear franchise and roughly $25 billion of just-awarded submarine work running to 2038, and capped by a 5.3% return on invested capital.
- Ingalls Shipbuilding (about 24%): roughly $3.75 billion of revenue at a 9.0% margin, about $338 million, at 11.0 times = $3.72 billion. Conventional surface combatants and amphibious ships, with the April 2026 frigate lead-yard-support contract and battleship advance procurement carried as modest optionality rather than in the numbers.
- Mission Technologies (about 24%): roughly $3.5 billion of revenue at a 9.0% margin -- consistent with the 8.4-8.6% guided for 2026 -- about $315 million, at 13.0 times = $4.10 billion, in line with defence-services and mission-systems peers rather than the higher multiple the unmanned portfolio alone might earn.
- Overlays: overfunded pension surplus about +$0.6 billion (the non-operating pension credit runs at roughly $170 million a year); capitalised net corporate cost about -$0.5 billion. Net +$0.1 billion.

Enterprise value $16.45 billion. Less net debt of $2.70 billion (from $2.92 billion today including capitalised leases; $2.69 billion excluding them) = equity of about $13.75 billion on roughly 39.3 million shares = $350 per share on the parts alone.

Cross-check on multiples: holding today's 11.5 times forward enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation constant onto 2028 consensus of $1.546 billion -- that is, pure earnings delivery with no re-rating -- gives about $384 per share. Splitting the parts-based $350 and the multiple-based $384 gives the base fair value of $370, about 14% above the current $324.21.
risk_reward: Poor at this price. Downside to the adverse case of $180 is $144 per share, about 44%. Upside to the base fair value of $370 is $46 per share, about 14%. The favourable case of $495 is 53% away but requires shipbuilding margin near 8.5% by 2028, which is well ahead of the 6.0-6.5% currently guided. In short, the business is improving on schedule but the shares have already discounted most of the near-term improvement: they jumped about 12% on the 30 July print and sit roughly 11% above their 50-day average of $292 and 25% above the 52-week low of $259. This is a good business at a fair price, not a good business at a good price.
catalyst_status_note: The load-bearing event has already happened. On 29 July 2026 the US Navy awarded $76.6 billion across nine Block VI Virginia-class attack submarines (with material for a tenth) and five Columbia-class Build II ballistic-missile submarines, with work running to July 2038 -- roughly $25 billion to HII's Newport News yard, about $5.5 billion on the Columbia programme, and about $5 billion shared with General Dynamics' Electric Boat for shipyard productivity, workforce and industrial-base investment. Management confirmed it on the 30 July 2026 earnings call ('an agreement has been reached on VCS Block VI and the next Columbia submarine contracts') and sized the Newport News share directly in response to an analyst question. The shares rose about 12% that day. This contract had slipped across four consecutive calls from mid-2025, so its signature removes the largest single overhang in the story -- but the re-rating it was going to cause has now largely been paid. Note that in this lane the status is descriptive only and carries no weight in the verdict; dated-event asymmetry is the separate catalyst book's job. Secondary, still-live milestones for the record: CVN 79 Kennedy preliminary acceptance later in 2026 (delivery 2027), SSN 800 Arkansas delivery late 2026, LPD 30 Harrisburg delivery in 2026, and ROMULUS unmanned surface vessel at-sea testing scheduled for September 2026.
peer_comps_note: Against the assigned true competitors, HII is the cheapest name in the chain and also the lowest-returning, which is the whole argument in one line. On trailing figures as of 4 August 2026: HII trades at 1.19 times enterprise value to sales and 14.1 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, with net debt at 2.6 times that measure, a 5.3% return on invested capital and a 12.9% return on equity. General Dynamics -- whose Electric Boat unit is the direct submarine peer and shares the same $76.6 billion award -- trades at 2.01 times sales and 17.1 times, with net debt at only 0.8 times, a 10.9% return on invested capital and a 17.4% return on equity. BWX Technologies, the naval nuclear reactor-components supplier one layer down the chain, trades at 5.13 times sales and 33.0 times, with a 27.9% return on equity but net debt at 3.7 times. Read plainly: General Dynamics earns roughly twice HII's return on capital and carries a third of the leverage, so its 17-times multiple is earned; BWX's 33 times prices a sole-source, high-margin component monopoly that HII's platform-integration position does not replicate. The 13 times applied to Newport News and 11 times to Ingalls in the base case sit deliberately below General Dynamics and far below BWX. International naval yards -- Babcock International, Fincantieri, Mitsubishi Heavy, Kawasaki, Austal -- have re-rated hard on European and AUKUS rearmament, which supports the direction of travel but not a premium multiple for a company earning 5% on capital. On forward numbers HII looks better: about 10.2 times consensus 2028 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, a genuine discount that closes only if the margin march reaches the 8% zone.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is subtler than usual, and it cuts both ways.

The street is wrong on the near term, in the company's favour. The two most recent published price targets were both set before the second-quarter result -- Bernstein at $337 on 17 July, when the stock was $271, and Wells Fargo at $325 on 8 July, when it was $289. Both are now at or below the traded price of $324.21. The published consensus of $360 rests on just two targets in the last quarter against nine over the past year, and the year-ago average was $369, so target velocity has been negative 10%. Consensus 2026 earnings per share of $17.80 is almost certainly stale: the first half already delivered $9.06, the second quarter beat by roughly 38%, and management raised both shipbuilding revenue and the margin floor. Our own build gets to roughly $19.15 for 2026. Those targets will be revised up over the next few weeks. That is a real, dateable dislocation -- but it is also the most crowded and shortest-lived kind, and about 12% of it was already taken on 30 July.

The street is also wrong, against the company, on the durability of the margin. The consensus 2028 earnings per share of $23.94 implies shipbuilding margin near 8%. Nothing in the transcripts supports that as a base case. Management has guided 6.0-6.5% for 2026 and describes the path as 'a nice incremental march' of roughly 30-40 basis points a year. On that cadence 8% arrives in 2030, not 2028. The chief financial officer was careful never to date the 9-10% ambition, and the chief executive's framing of the new submarine terms was pointedly deflationary: 'nothing really special... very consistent with the long term margin profile that we expect.' The market is extrapolating a straight line through four good quarters in a business where the previous four-quarter run ended with two single-session declines of 26% and 18%.

The third and largest disagreement is about cash. Consensus and management both carry 2026 free cash flow at $500-600 million. Almost nobody appears to have modelled what that requires: after a first half that consumed roughly $614 million and a third quarter guided to about $100 million, the fourth quarter must produce roughly $1.0-1.1 billion -- about double the $516 million achieved in the fourth quarter of 2025 -- and it depends on contract advances from a contract signed on 29 July plus a research-and-development tax credit. Analysts asked management to size the submarine contract adjustment twice on the last call and were refused twice. The company ended June with $12 million of cash. This is the assumption most likely to be factually wrong, and it breaks in February 2027, not now.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next three to nine months, and it has three distinct hazards.

First and largest, the fourth-quarter cash cliff. Free cash flow in the first half of 2026 was roughly negative $614 million: operating cash flow was negative $390 million in the first quarter and negative $31 million in the second, against net capital spending of $74 million and $119 million. The third quarter is guided to about $100 million. To hit the reiterated full-year range of $500-600 million, the fourth quarter must deliver roughly $1.0-1.1 billion -- roughly twice the $516 million achieved in the fourth quarter of 2025. Management's stated supports are 'meaningful positive cash impacts from contract advances and incentives' tied to a contract signed on 29 July, plus a research-and-development tax credit landing at year end. Contract advances are exactly the kind of item that slips a quarter on paperwork. The company ended June with a $12 million cash balance and $1.7 billion of liquidity that is therefore essentially all undrawn revolving credit, against net debt of $2.92 billion including capitalised leases. A miss means drawing the revolver and reporting it in February 2027, which is also when 2027 guidance is set.

Second, the estimate-at-completion risk. Reported profit under percentage-of-completion accounting is a judgement about costs four to six years away. Newport News took a negative 13% net estimate adjustment as recently as the third quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026 disclosed 'meaningful positive and negative adjustments' inside the carrier refuelling programme. The wage resets -- Newport News in mid-2025, the Ingalls collective bargaining agreement in March 2026 -- flow through the pre-pandemic contract book, which is still the majority of work in progress until 2027, with no escalation protection. This is where rising input costs actually bite an equipment maker: labour, not copper. A single adverse reset has twice produced a same-day decline of 18-26%.

Third, appropriations. The fiscal-2027 budget is a request, not law; management noted on 30 July that the House appropriations bill adds submarine industrial-base funding but 'we await the senate appropriations position, and final outcomes will depend on eventual respective conference committee negotiations.' The federal fiscal year turns on 1 October 2026. The previous lapse in October 2025 spared shipbuilding only because it was designated one of six departmental priorities -- a policy choice, not a guarantee -- and Mission Technologies, the segment most exposed to services funding, already shrank 3.9% year over year in the second quarter. A protracted continuing resolution into 2027 delays the CVN 82 and frigate awards that underpin the medium-term ramp.

A fourth, smaller hazard: three named delivery milestones all land inside this window -- CVN 79 Kennedy preliminary acceptance, SSN 800 Arkansas delivery, and LPD 30 Harrisburg delivery, all 'later this year.' Shipbuilding milestones slip routinely; management already moved LHA 8 Bougainville from 2026 to 2027. Any of the three slipping would puncture the throughput narrative at exactly the moment the market has started paying for it.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling dynamic here, and that is a genuine weakness of the setup rather than a comfort.

HII pays a quarterly dividend of $1.38 per share, about $55 million a quarter, for a yield of roughly 1.7%. It is well covered on earnings, it has not been cut, and there is no sign in any of the six calls that it is under review. So there is no mechanical income-fund liquidation to buy into. Equally, there is no pivot, no equity issuance, no index migration and no strategic process that would rotate the register.

What the shareholder base does have is a documented tendency to panic on estimate resets rather than to sell mechanically. On 31 October 2024 the shares fell 26% in one session, from $250.49 to $184.96, on volume of 2.6 million shares against a typical 300,000-400,000. On 6 February 2025 they fell another 18% on 2.4 million shares. That is discretionary capitulation by a concentrated, thinly covered holder base -- only two analysts published targets last quarter, and average daily traded value is about $75 million on a $12.8 billion market capitalisation, so the float clears slowly when everyone wants out at once. The same mechanism worked in reverse on 30 July 2026, when the stock rose about 12%.

The practical implication is that the wash-out to wait for is an earnings event, not a flow event. Insider behaviour offers no support in the meantime: zero open-market purchases against four sales totalling 14,100 shares, and the company itself repurchased nothing in the second quarter of 2026 and only $43 million in the first, despite trading roughly 30% below its 52-week high for much of that period. Management is spending its cash on the yards and the dividend, not on the shares. A company that will not buy its own stock at $270 is not telling you the stock is cheap at $324.
forcing_function:
The event that would have forced a re-rating already happened: the $76.6 billion Navy submarine award on 29 July 2026, disclosed on the earnings call the following morning, which lifted the shares about 12%. What remains are confirmations rather than catalysts, and they are dated.

- Third-quarter 2026 results, late October 2026. This is the first print that books the roughly $25 billion of Newport News submarine modifications into backlog, taking it from $57.3 billion toward roughly $80 billion, about six times annual revenue. It is also the quarter management said carries 'additional incentives that come about with the award.' Watch the net estimate-at-completion adjustment line at Newport News more than the headline.
- CVN 79 Kennedy preliminary acceptance, guided for 'later this year' with final delivery in 2027, and SSN 800 Arkansas and LPD 30 Harrisburg deliveries, both guided for late 2026. Three of the five ships management has committed to deliver over twelve months.
- ROMULUS unmanned surface vessel at-sea testing under the Navy medium unmanned surface vessel programme, scheduled for September 2026 -- the first real proof point for the autonomy franchise that currently carries no value in guidance.
- Fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 results, early February 2027. The decisive date. It settles whether the fourth quarter delivered the roughly $1.0-1.1 billion of free cash flow the guide requires, and it is when 2027 guidance is set -- including, for the first time, a shipbuilding margin number that reflects the new contracts. A shipbuilding margin guide with a 7 in front of it would validate the entire normalisation thesis; a repeat of 6.0-6.5% would say the march has stalled.
- Fiscal-2027 appropriations conference, autumn 2026 into early 2027, which determines the CVN 82 advance procurement, the first FFX frigate and the new battleship programme -- the three items management has deliberately kept out of guidance.

Note also that the two published price targets predate the second-quarter result and sit at or below the traded price. Target revisions over the coming weeks are a near-certain but low-value event; they follow the price, they do not lead it.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a genuinely good business improving on schedule, which has already been paid for. Wait for the wash-out rather than buying today.

Start with what is not in doubt. Huntington Ingalls is the only builder of nuclear-powered aircraft carriers in the United States and one of two builders of nuclear submarines, and on 29 July 2026 it secured its share of a $76.6 billion Navy award running to July 2038 -- roughly $25 billion at Newport News plus about $5 billion of customer-funded industrial-base investment shared with General Dynamics' Electric Boat. Backlog was $57.3 billion at 30 June, about 4.3 times revenue, before that award books in the third quarter. The forensic record is clean: every one of the three operational initiatives management set out in May 2025 has been delivered -- 14% throughput improvement, $250 million of cost taken out, and now the contracts signed. When they missed the throughput target they cut it in public mid-year rather than restating the base later. When Goldman Sachs tested whether the pre-pandemic-to-post-pandemic contract crossover had drifted, the answer was a falsifiable 'they look on top of each other right now.' Guidance was raised twice in the same release on 30 July. Credibility here is high, and the margin trend is real: shipbuilding return on sales 5.2%, then 5.9%, now guided 6.0-6.5%, with the quarterly sequence marching 5.8%, 6.0%, 6.3%.

On pricing power, the lie detector reads honest but thin. Gross margin expanded to 12.56% on a trailing-twelve-month basis from 12.38% a year earlier while revenue grew about 14% -- expansion on growing volume, not commoditisation bought with volume. But 0.2 percentage points is a whisper, and the improvement is driven by contract mix and incentive fees rather than by price. This company is a price-taker to a single buyer; that is why a business with impassable barriers earns only 5.3% on invested capital against General Dynamics' 10.9%. The moat is narrow in the only sense that matters to a shareholder: the barriers are absolute, the surplus is captured by the customer.

The order book is the strongest part of the case and it is dated properly. Second-quarter book-to-bill was 1.96 times, these are firm contracts with a sovereign counterparty rather than framework agreements, and the milestones are named and scheduled -- CVN 79 preliminary acceptance, SSN 800 and LPD 30 deliveries all in 2026, CVN 81 keel later this year, five ships over twelve months. The one place undated language does appear -- the Hyundai Heavy Industries partnership, which progressed from a memorandum of understanding to a memorandum of agreement over five quarters and produced nothing -- I have valued at zero, as should everyone.

Capital discipline is adequate rather than exemplary. Capital spending is running at 3.5-4% of sales against a 2.5% long-run norm, and it is growth capital for submarine throughput, much of it customer-funded through the $5 billion industrial-base tranche -- that is the right kind of spending. But the company bought back nothing in the second quarter and only $43 million in the first, while the shares traded 30-40% below their high. Management is not signalling that the stock is cheap.

The regime read is neutral for this chain, and I will not lean on it. What I will lean on is the input-cost path the bear case has to price, because for a shipbuilder it is labour rather than metal: HII reset wages at Newport News in mid-2025 and signed a new Ingalls labour agreement in March 2026, and every dollar of that above the assumptions baked into existing contract estimates lands as a charge on the pre-pandemic book that runs until 2027. That is precisely the mechanism that took the shares down 26% in one session on 31 October 2024 and a further 18% on 6 February 2025 -- a 36% decline in three months. It has been quiet for four quarters. It has not been retired.

Which brings me to the two numbers that decide this. Free cash flow in the first half of 2026 was roughly negative $614 million, the third quarter is guided to about $100 million, and the reiterated full-year guide of $500-600 million therefore requires roughly $1.0-1.1 billion in the fourth quarter alone -- about double what the fourth quarter of 2025 produced -- resting on contract advances from a contract signed on 29 July. The company ended June with $12 million of cash. Separately, our own screener proxy reports trailing free cash flow of $376 million and annual capital spending of $29 million; both are wrong, and materially so, since capital spending was $119 million in the second quarter alone. Anyone sizing on the proxy is sizing on a fiction.

Valuation reconciles to about $370 per share on a two-year view: the parts, valued on 2028-2029 earnings at 13 times for Newport News, 11 times for Ingalls and 13 times for Mission Technologies, come to $350; holding today's forward multiple constant onto 2028 consensus gives $384. That is 14% above the current $324.21. The adverse case, assuming a funding lapse flattens the ramp and the labour reset produces contract charges, is $180 -- a 44% fall, which is exactly the drawdown the shares actually suffered over the past twelve months from $460 to $259. The favourable case of $497 needs shipbuilding margin near 8.5% by 2028, well ahead of the current 6.0-6.5% and of management's own 'incremental march' cadence.

So: roughly 14% up to fair value against 44% down to the adverse case, on a stock that jumped 12% on the last print and sits 11% above its 50-day average. The business deserves a place on the list; the price does not deserve capital today. I would enter on either of two specific developments. The first is a level: $270 or below, which is the pre-print price and takes the discount to fair value from 12% to roughly 27%, giving a genuinely asymmetric setup. The second is a fact: a 2027 shipbuilding margin guide with a 7 in front of it, delivered in early February 2027 alongside a fourth quarter that actually produced its $1 billion of cash. Either would justify a full position. Until one of them arrives, this is a watch, not a buy.

One last note for the record: the submarine award has already fired, and in this lane that is neither a mark against the name nor a reason to chase it. Post-event franchises frequently keep running. My hesitation is about the price paid, not the spent catalyst.
